children: Oracle stock fell Monday after the software giant spelled out the details of a previously announced plan to raise $20 billion to help fund its artificial-intelligence infrastructure expansion.

The company disclosed in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing it would issue a $10 billion stock offering in addition to a $10 billion debt offering. Proceeds will go toward "general corporate purposes," such as capital expenditures, debt repayments, or future investments.
Just days earlier at its investor day event, Oracle committed to limiting additional capital raises through fiscal 2030.
The company is now moving to raise that entire amount at once, rather than spreading the fund-raising across the coming years.

Oracle shares fell 6.5% to $122.10, putting the stock on track for its lowest close since hitting $117.74 in July, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Shares are down 36% in 2026, on pace for their worst year since 2001, but are up 8.4% since hitting a 52-week closing low of $114.99 in July.
An acceleration in spending could renew concerns about the mounting costs of Oracle's AI expansion, which has required enormous investments in data centers and computing equipment to meet demand.

Oracle has increasingly relied on outside financing to support that expansion. In its first-quarter earnings report in September, Oracle disclosed $125.3 billion in outstanding borrowings as of Aug. 31, alongside $288 billion in additional lease commitments, largely tied to data centers, that had not yet be reflected on its balance sheet.

Oracle's fund-raising comes as Wall Street's concerns have swelled about the financing that technology companies are pouring into AI infrastructure and whether those investments will generate sufficient returns.
Those worries contributed to a selloff in technology stocks in October, as companies including Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms outlined increasingly ambitious spending plans.
Last week, Oracle sought to reassure investors that its spending will eventually pay off.

The company projected that it would generate positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028, rising to at least $30 billion in fiscal 2029, as its AI infrastructure investments begin generating returns.
